column1: # rule|intent|action|question
repetition.expansion|present|Recall one recent invitation and whether it left both people free to decline.|Where is curiosity creating room for connection, and where is it becoming an expectation?

repetition.expansion|crossroads|Compare the smallest invitation each option would involve, including what either person could decline.|Which possibility can you explore without promising a level of closeness you cannot offer?
repetition.expansion|action|Make one modest invitation with a clear scope and an easy way to decline.|What could you learn from the exchange without treating acceptance as proof of affection?
repetition.boundaries|present|Write down one limit in the relationship and whose need it currently protects.|Can both people say no, or does the arrangement protect only one person’s comfort?
repetition.boundaries|crossroads|For each option, name one boundary you would need to communicate before agreeing.|Which choice allows a willing yes without requiring you to hide an important limit?

repetition.boundaries|action|State one limit as what you can offer and what you cannot, without demanding agreement.|What need does this limit protect, and how can you explain it without assigning blame?

repetition.connection|present|Recall one recent exchange of help and note who asked, who offered and what was actually useful.|Where is support moving both ways, and where are you relying on an unspoken expectation?

repetition.connection|crossroads|Compare whose participation each option requires and which agreements have actually been made.|What would mutual participation look like for each choice, beyond hoping the other person agrees?

repetition.connection|action|Ask for one manageable form of support, or check whether a specific offer would be welcome.|How can you make room for an honest response instead of assuming the exchange should happen?

repetition.solitude|present|Notice what your last period of time apart clarified and what still needs a conversation.|Is private reflection helping you understand a need, or keeping that need out of reach?

repetition.solitude|crossroads|Compare how much space each option allows you to think without pressure, and how you would reconnect.|Which choice supports independence while leaving a usable way to communicate?
repetition.solitude|action|Take ten quiet minutes to name one need; decide whether and when to bring it into a conversation.|What is ready to be shared after reflection, and what can remain private?
repetition.clarity|present|Write one thing the person actually said beside the meaning you added to it.|Which part of your understanding comes from the exchange, and which part is an inference?

repetition.clarity|crossroads|Apply the same evidence standard to both options: note what was agreed and what you are assuming.|What fact would change your comparison rather than merely confirm the option you prefer?

repetition.clarity|action|Draft one direct question about an unclear agreement, then ask it when a conversation is welcome.|What would a clear answer help you decide without asking the person to prove how they feel?

repetition.uncertainty|present|Name one unanswered question about the relationship and separate it from a story about the other person’s motives.|Which uncertainty concerns something you can ask, and which concerns an inner state you cannot know?

repetition.uncertainty|crossroads|For each option, mark one unknown that could change your decision and one that can remain open.|How much uncertainty can you accept without pretending an agreement already exists?

repetition.uncertainty|action|Choose one unknown and prepare an answerable question, leaving room for the person to need time or decline.|What can you decide for yourself if that question remains unanswered?

repetition.change|present|Identify one recurring arrangement that no longer fits how either person’s circumstances have changed.|What has changed in the relationship, rather than only in your expectations of it?

repetition.change|crossroads|Compare what each option would revise and what you would want to preserve in the relationship.|Which change addresses the present situation without requiring you to dismiss what mattered before?
repetition.change|action|Propose one adjustment to a shared routine and ask whether it would work for the other person.|What would you observe before keeping, revising or dropping that adjustment?

repetition.stability|present|Notice one ordinary act of follow-through that currently makes the relationship dependable.|What creates trust in daily practice, beyond a promise or an occasional significant gesture?
repetition.stability|crossroads|Compare the everyday commitments each option requires, including who would maintain them.|Which arrangement could remain dependable on an ordinary difficult day?

repetition.stability|action|Choose one small commitment you can realistically keep and communicate its scope.|What would make that follow-through useful without turning it into an unlimited obligation?

repetition.effort|present|Recall one effort you made toward connection and distinguish its actual effect from the response you hoped for.|Where is effort helping an exchange, and where is it trying to control the outcome?

repetition.effort|crossroads|Compare the effort each option asks of you and whether the necessary participation has been discussed.|Which effort serves a shared purpose rather than requiring you to carry the whole exchange?

repetition.effort|action|Spend ten minutes preparing one clear request or completing one agreed task, then stop and review.|What did your action make clearer without requiring a particular response from the other person?
repetition.rest|present|Notice one conversation or obligation that becomes harder when your attention is depleted.|What needs a genuine pause before it can be understood fairly?

repetition.rest|crossroads|Compare which demands can wait under each option and how you would communicate a pause.|Which choice leaves room to recover without leaving an important commitment unexplained?

repetition.rest|action|Remove one nonessential demand and, if someone is waiting on you, name when you can respond again.|What would make this pause restorative rather than another way of staying under pressure?
repetition.care|present|Name one need for support, including your own, and check whether the support currently offered meets it.|Whose needs are easy to notice, and whose are being assumed away?

repetition.care|crossroads|Compare what each option asks people to give and receive, including support that has not been agreed.|Which arrangement makes care available without assuming anyone has unlimited capacity?

repetition.care|action|Ask what support would help, or name a support need of your own, before offering another task.|What could be received, reduced or shared instead of simply adding more care work?

repetition.release|present|Name one expectation you are still carrying and whether it remains useful to the relationship.|Are you keeping this expectation by choice, or because you have already invested in it?

repetition.release|crossroads|For each option, identify what you would relinquish and any responsibility that would still need attention.|What can end without treating the relationship’s earlier meaning as a mistake?

repetition.release|action|Set aside one outdated expectation; if it affects an agreement, discuss the change instead of silently withdrawing.|What space becomes available when you stop asking the present to repeat the past?

tension.expansion-boundaries|present|Notice one invitation you want to make and one limit that would keep it voluntary for both people.|Where could there be more openness without giving up the right to decline?

tension.expansion-boundaries|crossroads|Compare how each option handles both a request for closeness and a request for space; mark what has not been discussed.|Which limits need to be understood before either choice could be made freely?

tension.expansion-boundaries|action|Make one modest invitation with a clear scope and an easy way to decline; change your own action rather than testing the person.|What could you offer without treating acceptance as proof of how they feel?

tension.connection-solitude|present|Recall a recent period apart and notice what it clarified versus what still needed an exchange.|Where is distance helping you think, and where is it obscuring a need that could be named?

tension.connection-solitude|crossroads|Compare how each option makes room for private reflection and for a clear return to conversation.|What amount of independence would let you choose honestly without cutting off useful exchange?
tension.connection-solitude|action|Ask for a short period to think and offer a specific time to return to the conversation.|What do you want to understand privately before you can share it clearly?
tension.change-stability|present|Identify one shared routine that helps and one part of it that no longer fits current circumstances.|What needs revision, and what still provides dependable support?

tension.change-stability|crossroads|For each option, note one support you would preserve and one arrangement you would need to renegotiate.|Which change can you make without abandoning the support that makes it manageable?
tension.change-stability|action|Propose changing one part of a shared routine while keeping one useful commitment steady.|What would show that the adjustment helps both continuity and room to change?

tension.effort-rest|present|Notice one place where trying harder is making a conversation less attentive rather than more useful.|What part of the difficulty comes from the issue itself, and what part from depleted capacity?

tension.effort-rest|crossroads|Compare what each option asks you to do now and what could wait until you have more attention.|Which commitment can you sustain without treating recovery as something you must earn?

tension.effort-rest|action|Choose one small agreed task or brief conversation, name a stopping point, and take a real pause afterward.|What amount of effort helped before your attention began to deteriorate?

tension.clarity-uncertainty|present|Write down one thing the person actually said and the meaning you added; mark what remains unconfirmed.|Which part of your understanding comes from an exchange, and which part are you filling in?

tension.clarity-uncertainty|crossroads|For each option, note one assumption about the other person that would change your choice; prepare a direct question rather than guessing.|What do you need to clarify before either choice would be an informed commitment?

tension.clarity-uncertainty|action|Choose one uncertain point and draft a direct, answerable question; leave room for the person to decline or need time.|What could this conversation clarify without requiring a particular response?
tension.care-boundaries|present|List one form of support you are giving or receiving and the limit that keeps it freely chosen.|Where has care become an obligation that no one has checked with you?

tension.care-boundaries|crossroads|Compare what each option asks you to give, receive and stop carrying; include your own capacity before making another promise.|Which option leaves room for both care and an honest no?

tension.care-boundaries|action|Name one support need and one limit in the same sentence, then use it to make or revise a request.|What would make this exchange sustainable for you as well as the other person?

complement.clarity-effort|present|Notice whether your effort toward the relationship addresses a need that has actually been named.|What becomes simpler when you distinguish the agreed need from the response you hope to obtain?

complement.clarity-effort|crossroads|For each option, write the need it addresses and one feasible action it would require; flag any unconfirmed agreement.|Which effort follows from something you have clarified, rather than a promise you feel pressure to make?

complement.clarity-effort|action|Clarify one request or limit first, then take one small action consistent with it and review what you learned.|Did the action honor what was clarified, or become another way to seek a particular response?
complement.care-connection|present|Recall one need that was noticed and check whether it became a useful exchange or an unspoken expectation.|Where could naming a need make support more reciprocal?

complement.care-connection|crossroads|Compare what support each option would need and whether the people involved have been asked about it.|Which choice allows care to become an agreement instead of assuming someone will provide it?

complement.care-connection|action|Name one need of your own or ask about one need of the other person, then discuss a manageable response together.|How can this exchange include both the person who needs support and the capacity of whoever provides it?

complement.release-change|present|Identify one outdated expectation that is taking up room needed for the relationship as it is now.|What are you trying to preserve through that expectation, and could it take a different form?

complement.release-change|crossroads|Compare what each possible change requires you to stop carrying, including any agreement that needs a clear ending.|Which option creates room deliberately instead of adding a new demand on top of an exhausted one?
complement.release-change|action|Discuss ending or reducing one outdated commitment before proposing what might replace it.|What would make the next change a choice rather than another obligation?
